body.text: IRC Section 174 governs the federal tax treatment of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures for U.S. businesses. After the TCJA required five-year domestic and 15-year foreign amortization for 2022–2024, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's new Section 174A restored immediate domestic expensing for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, while foreign R&E remains amortized over 15 years.
Executive Summary and Legislative Evolution

Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174 governs the federal income tax treatment of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures, serving as a foundational mechanism in United States tax policy for regulating the after-tax cost of technological and industrial innovation. Originally enacted as part of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (P.L. 83-591), Section 174 was designed to resolve long-standing judicial and administrative ambiguity regarding whether research costs represented current ordinary and necessary business expenses deductible under Section 162 or capital outlays that had to be assigned to the basis of a resulting asset with an indeterminate useful life. Prior to 1954, taxpayers faced acute uncertainty over when failed or ongoing research costs could be recovered if no depreciable asset materialized, which disproportionately penalized early-stage enterprises and capital-intensive laboratories whose multi-year experimental programs lacked guaranteed commercial outcomes. To eliminate this ambiguity and subsidize the inherent technical risk of innovation, the 1954 statute created a statutory safe harbor permitting taxpayers either to deduct R&E expenditures immediately in the taxable year paid or incurred or to elect to capitalize and amortize those expenditures over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realized benefits from the expenditures.

For nearly seven decades, immediate expensing under Section 174 lowered the after-tax cost of capital for research-intensive enterprises across the aerospace, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, and software sectors, aligning federal tax policy with the macroeconomic principle that technological progress drives long-term productivity and economic growth. That paradigm shifted fundamentally with the enactment of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017 (P.L. 115-97, Section 13206). As a base-broadening revenue offset designed to help finance the permanent reduction of the federal corporate income tax rate to 21% within the ten-year budget reconciliation window, Congress amended Section 174 on a delayed basis, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Under the TCJA regime, taxpayers were prohibited from immediately deducting R&E expenditures and were instead required to capitalize all specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures and amortize them ratably over five years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research, beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenses were paid or incurred. Because the statutory midpoint convention allows only a half-year of amortization in the initial year, a five-year domestic amortization period actually spans six taxable years (10% in Year 1, 20% in Years 2 through 5, and 10% in Year 6), while a 15-year foreign amortization period spans 16 taxable years (3.33% in Year 1, 6.67% in Years 2 through 15, and 3.33% in Year 16). This front-loaded deferral created severe cash-flow compression and generated artificial positive taxable income for pre-profit startups, software developers, and research-intensive firms operating at a book loss.

In July 2025, the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21) restructured the statutory framework once again by introducing IRC Section 174A while retaining a modified version of Section 174. Effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, Section 174A permanently restores immediate expensing (or elective amortization over not less than 60 months under Section 174A(c)) for domestic R&E expenditures, while Section 174 continues to mandate 15-year amortization for foreign R&E expenditures. By pairing an immediate 100% deduction for domestic research with a punitive 15-year recovery period and strict disposition locks for offshore research, Congress transformed the statutory framework from a neutral tax accounting provision into an explicit industrial policy instrument favoring the on-shoring of intellectual property development and engineering labor. In addition, the OBBBA and its implementing administrative guidance—IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28, issued August 28, 2025—establish a bifurcated transition regime: eligible small businesses meeting the $31,000,000 gross receipts threshold under Section 448(c) may elect to apply full domestic expensing retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, whereas all other taxpayers may elect to recover their unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E capital balances over either one year (in 2025) or two years (ratably across 2025 and 2026).

body.text: Statutory Architecture: Interplay Among Sections 174, 174A, 162, and 41

The operational mechanics of Section 174 and Section 174A cannot be evaluated in isolation; their compliance consequences and audit exposure are defined by their statutory boundaries with Section 162 (ordinary and necessary trade or business expenses) and Section 41 (the Credit for Increasing Research Activities). Understanding how costs flow through these interlocking provisions is essential for both corporate tax provision modeling and examination defense.
Section 174 versus Section 162: The "In Connection With" Standard

A foundational statutory distinction separates the deductibility threshold of Section 162 from that of Section 174 and Section 174A. Section 162(a) authorizes a deduction for all the ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in "carrying on" any trade or business. Under settled federal tax jurisprudence, the "carrying on" standard requires that the enterprise already be functioning as an active, operational business capable of generating commercial revenue; pre-opening or start-up expenditures incurred prior to the commencement of active business operations are barred from immediate deduction under Section 162 and must instead be capitalized under Section 195. Conversely, Section 174 and Section 174A apply to R&E expenditures paid or incurred "in connection with" the taxpayer's trade or business.

In Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), the United States Supreme Court held that the statutory phrase "in connection with" in Section 174 is purposefully broader and less restrictive than the "carrying on" standard of Section 162. The Supreme Court recognized that Congress enacted Section 174 specifically to encourage fledgling, pre-revenue enterprises to undertake risky scientific and technological development on an equal tax footing with established conglomerates that already possess active product lines. Consequently, a pre-revenue startup developing its initial hardware prototype, software platform, or therapeutic compound—which would otherwise be barred from deducting pre-operating expenses under Section 162 because it is not yet actively "carrying on" a trade or business—is entitled to deduct qualifying R&E expenditures immediately under Section 174A (or former Section 174). This statutory architecture enables pre-revenue enterprises to generate substantial Net Operating Losses (NOLs) during their multi-year development phase that can be carried forward indefinitely under Section 172 to shelter future commercial income once products reach the market.

During the 2022–2024 mandatory capitalization window under the TCJA, however, this broad statutory scope inverted from a taxpayer benefit into an acute source of compliance friction. Because Section 174 treatment was mandatory rather than elective for all expenditures meeting the definition of specified research or experimental outlays, corporate taxpayers sought to reclassify research, engineering, and software development costs as ordinary Section 162 operational expenses to preserve immediate deductibility and avoid five-year or 15-year amortization. The Internal Revenue Service maintained a strict enforcement posture that Section 174 is not an elective safe harbor when an expenditure satisfies the regulatory criteria of Treasury Regulations Section 1.174-2 or the software development mandate of Section 174(c)(3): any expenditure incurred for the elimination of technical uncertainty or software development falls exclusively within Section 174 (and post-2024 Section 174A for domestic activities) regardless of how the taxpayer characterizes the cost on its financial statements. Under the post-OBBBA regime, this classification tension persists with full force for multinational enterprises utilizing offshore engineering teams, where characterizing foreign technical labor as routine Section 162 maintenance rather than Section 174 research or software development determines whether the expenditure is deducted immediately or locked into a 15-year amortization schedule.

body.text: Section 174 and Section 41: The Qualification Funnel

The relationship between Section 174/174A and the Section 41 R&D Tax Credit operates as a two-stage qualification funnel in which Section 174/174A represents the wide outer boundary of eligible research activities and costs, while Section 41 functions as a narrow spout isolating a specific subset of direct domestic expenses for tax credit computation. Under IRC Section 41(d), an activity qualifies for the research credit only if it satisfies all four cumulative criteria of the statutory Four-Part Test. First, under the Section 174 Test, the expenditure must be eligible for treatment as a research or experimental cost under Section 174 or, for post-2024 domestic expenditures, Section 174A. Second, under the Technological in Nature requirement, the activity must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Permitted Purpose standard, the activity must be intended to discover information useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer—defined rigorously as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business—specifically with respect to function, performance, reliability, or quality. Fourth, under the Elimination of Uncertainty and Process of Experimentation prong, substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to eliminate technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design.

Even where a research project satisfies every element of the Four-Part Test, the expenditure categories captured by Section 174 and Section 174A are substantially broader than those eligible for the Section 41 tax credit. Section 174/174A encompasses both direct research outlays and indirect overhead costs allocable to research activities—including laboratory and server-room rent, utilities, depreciation or amortization of research equipment, legal and patent prosecution fees incurred in perfecting research-derived intellectual property, and 100% of third-party contractor expenses—as well as all software development costs under Section 174(c)(3) regardless of whether they satisfy the Section 41 process-of-experimentation standard. Conversely, Section 41(b) restricts "Qualified Research Expenses" (QREs) strictly to three direct expenditure categories incurred in the United States: in-house wages (Form W-2 box 1 taxable wages, or self-employment earned income) for employees directly engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research; supplies (tangible property other than land, improvements to land, or depreciable property) consumed directly in the conduct of qualified research; and 65% of contract research expenses paid to unrelated third parties (increased to 75% or 100% for certain payments to qualified research consortia, universities, or eligible small businesses), along with eligible cloud computing rental or lease costs used directly in software development and research hosting environments.

Because of these statutory exclusions from QREs—most notably indirect overhead, facilities, equipment depreciation, patent legal fees, the 35% haircut on third-party contractor costs, and all foreign research activities—a taxpayer's Section 174/174A expenditure total always exceeds its Section 41 QRE total. In a representative software enterprise scenario, a company might incur $2,000,000 in total Section 174/174A expenditures once server-room rent, allocable facility overhead, patent prosecution legal costs, routine feature coding, and 100% of contractor expenses are aggregated, yet qualify for only $1,200,000 in Section 41 QREs limited to direct engineering wages, cloud development hosting, and 65% of eligible domestic contract research. During the 2022–2024 TCJA capitalization period, this structural divergence forced firms to capitalize the larger $2,000,000 Section 174 pool over five or 15 years while claiming a tax credit calculated solely on the narrower $1,200,000 Section 41 base. In the post-OBBBA audit environment, the Internal Revenue Service frequently cross-examines a taxpayer's Section 174/174A schedules against its Form 6765 Section 41 QRE filings; an abnormally small gap between Section 174/174A costs and Section 41 QREs serves as an immediate audit flag indicating either that indirect overhead and non-qualifying software development were improperly omitted from Section 174/174A or that non-qualifying indirect expenses were erroneously inflated into the Section 41 QRE base.
Regulatory Scope of Research and Experimental Expenditures

Treasury Regulations Section 1.174-2 (26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2) provides the authoritative regulatory definition of what constitutes a research or experimental expenditure. Mastering the technical nuances of these regulations is essential for corporate tax compliance, particularly given the sharp divergence in tax recovery between domestic research under Section 174A (100% immediate deduction) and foreign research under Section 174 (mandatory 15-year amortization) following the enactment of the OBBBA.
The Uncertainty Standard and Failed Projects

Under Treasury Regulations Section 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures qualify as R&E costs if they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense. Expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are directed at activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product, process, formula, invention, pilot model, or similar property. Under the regulations, uncertainty exists whenever the information available to the taxpayer does not establish either the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the appropriate design of that product.

This regulatory standard encompasses both fundamental "blue sky" research aimed at discovering entirely new scientific or engineering technologies and applied research focused on enhancing an existing product's performance, reliability, functionality, or quality. Crucially, qualification under Section 174 and Section 174A is governed entirely by the nature of the activity—the systematic attempt to eliminate technical uncertainty—rather than the subsequent commercial viability or scientific success of the venture. Consequently, costs associated with failed research projects ("dry holes") are fully governed by Section 174 and Section 174A.

The tax treatment of failed or abandoned R&E projects highlights one of the most punitive aspects of the Section 174 capitalization architecture. Prior to the TCJA, if a taxpayer elected to capitalize R&E costs over 60 months under former Section 174(b) and subsequently abandoned the project, the unamortized basis could generally be recovered immediately as an abandonment loss under IRC Section 165. Under the TCJA rules in force from 2022 through 2024, however, Congress enacted Section 174(d), which expressly barred taxpayers from claiming any deduction on account of the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of property with respect to which specified research or experimental expenditures were paid or incurred, requiring continued amortization over the original five-year or 15-year schedule even after the project was terminated or the underlying subsidiary was liquidated. Under the OBBBA, while domestic R&E is once again deductible immediately under Section 174A (eliminating unamortized basis for expensed domestic projects), Congress amended Section 174(d) with respect to foreign research to provide that for any property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, no loss deduction or basis offset is permitted for the unamortized foreign R&E basis, and amortization must continue inexorably across the remainder of the 15-year statutory period.
Software Development Under Section 174(c)(3) and Notice 2023-63

The TCJA added Section 174(c)(3), which mandates that any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software shall be treated as a research or experimental expenditure. By establishing software development as a per se statutory R&E category—a classification carried forward into Section 174A for domestic software development post-2024—Congress effectively removed the regulatory "uncertainty" threshold for software: if an activity constitutes software development, its associated direct and indirect costs automatically fall within Section 174 or Section 174A regardless of whether technical design, capability, or method uncertainty is present.

To assist taxpayers in separating statutory software development from routine operational maintenance—building upon legacy administrative principles established in Revenue Procedure 2000-50—the Internal Revenue Service issued substantive interim guidance in Notice 2023-63. Under Notice 2023-63, software development encompasses planning the development of computer software, designing the computer software or upgrades and enhancements, building a model of the computer software, writing source code and converting it to machine-readable code, and testing the software or upgrades and enhancements up to the point the software is placed in service or ready for commercial release, including the conversion of legacy systems where new source code is written. Conversely, software maintenance consists of post-release activities that do not create upgrades or functional enhancements, such as routine debugging to correct flaws and restore software to its original operational specifications, performing corrective maintenance, or configuring and installing purchased off-the-shelf software packages without modifying the underlying source code.

For Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) and technology enterprises, this regulatory boundary imposes a rigorous engineering documentation burden. Under modern Agile and continuous-integration software engineering workflows, development sprints routinely commingle new feature coding with production bug fixes. Every development sprint, epic, and work ticket (such as Jira tracking logs) must be evaluated to determine whether it represents routine post-release maintenance and debugging immediately deductible under Section 162, or a feature enhancement governed by Section 174/174A. While both Section 162 maintenance and Section 174A software development are immediately deductible when performed domestically after December 31, 2024, the distinction remains critical for three reasons: first, any software development performed by foreign employees or offshore contractors must be capitalized over 15 years under Section 174, whereas offshore routine maintenance remains immediately deductible under Section 162; second, domestic Section 174A software development deductions are subject to the Section 280C(c) reduction rules when claiming the Section 41 credit, whereas Section 162 maintenance expenses are outside Section 280C(c); and third, during open audits of the 2022–2024 tax years for large taxpayers, separating Section 162 maintenance from Section 174(c)(3) software development directly governs the size of the mandatory capitalization pool.
Regulatory Exclusions Under Treasury Regulations Section 1.174-2

Treasury Regulations Section 1.174-2(a)(6) expressly excludes several categories of business activities from Section 174 and Section 174A treatment, allowing those operational outlays to be deducted currently under Section 162 or recovered under separate capital provisions. Specifically, the ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control—verifying that commercial production units comply with established engineering specifications—is excluded from R&E classification, as are efficiency surveys, management studies, and operational workflow reorganizations directed at business processes rather than technological development. Similarly, consumer surveys, advertising, promotions, and market research incurred to assess customer preferences or commercial feasibility fall outside Section 174/174A, alongside research in connection with literary, historical, or similar non-technological projects.

Finally, the regulations draw a sharp legal boundary regarding intellectual property acquisition versus internal development. Legal and administrative fees expended by a taxpayer in making and perfecting a patent application resulting from the taxpayer's own R&E activities are explicitly included within Section 174/174A as direct costs of obtaining the patent. By contrast, the costs of acquiring another party's existing patent, model, production, or process are excluded from Section 174/174A and must instead be capitalized and amortized ratably over 15 years as an acquired Section 197 intangible asset (or depreciated over the asset's useful life under Section 167 if acquired separately from a trade or business).
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025: Structural Reforms and Transition Rules

The enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21) in July 2025 marked a watershed shift in federal R&D tax policy, repealing the mandatory five-year capitalization regime for domestic research that had been in effect since January 1, 2022, while permanently codifying the 15-year amortization penalty for foreign research.
Section 174A: Permanent Expensing and Elective Amortization for Domestic R&E

The OBBBA enacted IRC Section 174A, which explicitly authorizes the immediate deduction of "domestic research or experimental expenditures" paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. For purposes of Section 174A, domestic research is defined geographically to encompass any research or experimental activity (including software development) conducted within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States. The geographic determination hinges on the physical location where the research services and experimental activities are performed, rather than the place of incorporation of the entity paying for the research or the legal situs where the resulting intellectual property is registered.

While immediate deduction is the statutory default under Section 174A(a), Congress also enacted Section 174A(c), which permits taxpayers to elect to capitalize domestic R&E expenditures and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. An election under Section 174A(c) must be made no later than the time prescribed by law for filing the tax return for the taxable year (including extensions) and is binding for the taxable year in which it is made and for all subsequent taxable years unless the taxpayer secures the prior consent of the Secretary of the Treasury (via the Internal Revenue Service) to revoke the election. Additionally, taxpayers retain the targeted projective election under IRC Section 59(e) to capitalize and amortize all or a specific dollar portion of otherwise deductible Section 174A expenditures ratably over 10 years, which applies on an annual, year-by-year basis without binding subsequent years. These elective capitalization mechanisms provide vital strategic flexibility for corporations with expiring general business credits, Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT) exposure under Section 59A, foreign-derived intangible income (FDII) deduction optimization under Section 250, or interest deductibility limits under Section 163(j) that seek to defer R&E deductions in order to manage current-year taxable income levels.
Retention of the 15-Year Foreign Research Penalty

In contrast to its restoration of domestic expensing, the OBBBA retained the TCJA's mandatory capitalization regime under Section 174(a)(2)(B) for foreign research. All R&E expenditures attributable to research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and U.S. possessions must be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 15-year period beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenditures are paid or incurred. This statutory asymmetry creates a pronounced after-tax cost wedge between domestic and offshore engineering talent.

To illustrate this disparity quantitatively under statutory rates, consider a U.S. corporation subject to the 21% federal corporate tax rate that hires a software developer in Austin, Texas, for a total compensation cost of $150,000 in 2025. Under Section 174A(a), the corporation is entitled to an immediate $150,000 deduction in Year 1, generating an immediate federal cash tax savings of $150,000 × 21% = $31,500. If the same corporation instead hires a software developer in London, United Kingdom (or contracts with an offshore development center in India or Eastern Europe) for $150,000 in 2025, the expenditure must be capitalized over 15 years under Section 174(a)(2)(B). This $5,000 Year 1 deduction yields a first-year cash tax benefit of only $5,000 × 21% = $1,050, followed by deductions of $10,000 per year ($2,100 tax savings per year) in Years 2 through 15 and the remaining $5,000 ($1,050 tax savings) in Year 16. At a standard corporate discount rate of 8%, the net present value of the tax shield from the foreign developer is eroded by nearly half compared to the domestic developer. Furthermore, because the OBBBA amended Section 174(d) for property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, to prohibit any loss deduction or basis recovery for unamortized foreign R&E basis, the taxpayer remains locked into the 16-calendar-year amortization schedule even if the offshore development project fails completely and is abandoned in Year 2.
Retroactive Relief for Eligible Small Businesses (2022–2024)

A central pillar of the OBBBA is its retroactive transition relief for "Eligible Small Businesses," defined by statutory cross-reference to the gross receipts test of IRC Section 448(c) as taxpayers (other than tax shelters prohibited from using the cash method under Section 448(a)(3)) whose average annual gross receipts for the three-taxable-year period ending with the taxable year preceding the first applicable taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, do not exceed $31,000,000. When applying the $31,000,000 threshold under Section 448(c), taxpayers must strictly apply the controlled group and affiliated service group aggregation rules of IRC Sections 52(a), 52(b), 414(m), and 414(o), requiring parent-subsidiary and brother-sister entities under common control (generally > 50% common ownership) to combine their gross receipts.

Eligible small businesses satisfying this threshold are permitted to elect to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. By exercising this election, a qualifying small business may amend its 2022, 2023, and 2024 federal income tax returns to reverse prior Section 174 capitalization and claim a 100% immediate deduction for domestic R&E expenditures in the taxable years originally paid or incurred. This provision effectively erases the cash-flow penalty of the TCJA capitalization era for qualifying small enterprises, generating substantial cash tax refunds (plus statutory interest where applicable) for profitable startups and small technology manufacturers that paid federal income tax between 2022 and 2024 solely because their R&D deductions were deferred. Under the OBBBA, this retroactive election must be executed within one year of the statute's July 2025 enactment—requiring all amended returns or administrative adjustment requests to be filed no later than July 2026.
Accelerated Basis Recovery for Large Taxpayers (2025 and 2026)

Taxpayers whose aggregated average annual gross receipts exceed the $31,000,000 Section 448(c) threshold (as well as eligible small businesses that choose not to bear the administrative cost of amending three prior years of returns) are barred from amending their 2022, 2023, and 2024 returns to claim retroactive refunds. Instead, the OBBBA establishes an accelerated prospective transition rule allowing all taxpayers to recover the remaining "stranded" unamortized basis of domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred during the 2022–2024 capitalization window. Under this transition mechanism, a taxpayer may elect to deduct 100% of its remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E basis in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (the 2025 tax return for calendar-year taxpayers), or alternatively elect to deduct that remaining unamortized basis ratably over two taxable years (50% in 2025 and 50% in 2026) to smooth the impact on financial statements, effective tax rates, and tax attributes.
Administrative Implementation: IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28

On August 28, 2025, the Internal Revenue Service issued Revenue Procedure 2025-28 to establish the detailed administrative procedures for executing retroactive small business elections, superseding 2024 returns, and filing automatic accounting method changes under the OBBBA.
Mechanics of the Small Business Retroactive Election

Revenue Procedure 2025-28 provides tailored procedural avenues for eligible small businesses electing retroactive domestic expensing under Section 174A across the 2022, 2023, and 2024 taxable years. For the 2022 and 2023 taxable years (and 2024 taxable years where the extended return due date has already elapsed), qualifying taxpayers must file federal amended returns—such as Form 1040-X for individuals, Form 1120-X for C corporations, Form 1120-S (with the amended return box checked) for S corporations, or an Administrative Adjustment Request (AAR) on Form 1065-X / Form 8082 for partnerships subject to the Bipartisan Budget Act (BBA) centralized partnership audit regime—to deduct previously capitalized domestic R&E costs and claim resulting tax refunds or restore Net Operating Losses.

For the 2024 taxable year, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 provides an important administrative relief mechanism: if a taxpayer filed its original 2024 return without an extension (or prior to the expiration of its extended filing deadline), Revenue Procedure 2025-28 grants an automatic six-month extension from the original due date that treats a subsequent return filed on or before the extended due date as a "superseding" return. Because a superseding return legally replaces the original filing in its entirety as the taxpayer's original timely filed return, eligible small businesses can implement immediate 2024 domestic expensing (or large taxpayers can finalize their 2024 capitalization schedules cleanly) without undergoing the multi-month administrative delays and manual review queues associated with processing an amended return or BBA partnership AAR. To perfect the small business retroactive election across any of these filings, the taxpayer must attach a formal election statement titled "Filed Pursuant to Section 3.03 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28" to the return, specifying the taxpayer's name, Employer Identification Number (or Social Security Number), a declaration that the taxpayer satisfies the Section 448(c) gross receipts test as an eligible small business, and the applicable taxable years covered by the retroactive election.
Automatic Accounting Method Changes and Modified Section 481(a) Adjustments

For large taxpayers (and non-amending small businesses) adopting Section 174A immediate expensing in 2025 and electing accelerated one-year or two-year recovery of their 2022–2024 domestic unamortized basis, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 authorizes an automatic change in method of accounting. Under general IRS accounting method rules set forth in Revenue Procedure 2015-13, Section 5.01(1)(f), taxpayers are prohibited from using the automatic consent procedures to change their method of accounting for the same item more than once within a five-year window ending with the year of change. Recognizing that successive statutory enactments under the TCJA (mandatory capitalization in 2022) and the OBBBA (restoration of domestic expensing in 2025) compelled taxpayers to alter their R&E accounting methods repeatedly between 2022 and 2025, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 explicitly waives the five-year prior-change scope limitation for changes made for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024.

Furthermore, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 coordinates the recovery of the unamortized 2022–2024 domestic basis through a modified IRC Section 481(a) adjustment (or simplified statement in lieu of Form 3115 for specified initial-year changes). Whereas standard voluntary accounting method changes require positive Section 481(a) adjustments (income increases) to be spread over four taxable years and negative Section 481(a) adjustments (deductions) to be taken entirely in the year of change, the OBBBA transition regime provides taxpayers an explicit statutory choice: the negative adjustment representing the unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E balance is deducted either 100% in the 2025 year of change or ratably across two taxable years (50% in 2025 and 50% in 2026) in accordance with the taxpayer's binding transition election.
Interaction with the Section 41 R&D Tax Credit and Section 280C(c)

The restoration of immediate domestic expensing under the OBBBA reinstates the traditional pre-TCJA optimization dynamics governing IRC Section 280C(c), which coordinates Section 174 and Section 174A deductions with the Section 41 R&D tax credit.
The Section 280C(c)(1) Reduction Rule versus the Section 280C(c)(3) Reduced Credit Election

To prevent a taxpayer from claiming a double tax benefit—both a full 100% deduction and a full tax credit—on the same dollar of domestic research expenditure, post-OBBBA Section 280C(c)(1) mandates that the taxpayer's domestic Section 174A deduction (or capitalized domestic R&E account) be reduced by 100% of the gross Section 41 research credit claimed for the taxable year. Reducing the deduction by the full gross credit increases federal taxable income dollar-for-dollar by the amount of the credit, which also flows through to increase state taxable income in states that begin their corporate tax computation with federal taxable income.

To avoid reducing the Section 174A deduction and simplify multi-state tax compliance, a taxpayer may elect under Section 280C(c)(3) on an original timely filed tax return (including extensions) to claim a reduced Section 41 credit. Under Section 280C(c)(3), the gross Section 41 credit is reduced by the maximum corporate tax rate in effect under Section 11(b)—currently 21%—leaving the taxpayer with 100% − 21% = 79% of the gross credit while preserving 100% of its Section 174A deduction.

To demonstrate the mathematical equivalence and state-tax divergence of these two statutory pathways, consider a domestic C corporation subject to the 21% federal tax rate that incurs $1,000,000 in domestic R&E expenses in 2025 and generates a $100,000 gross Section 41 R&D credit. Under the standard rule of Section 280C(c)(1) where no election is made, the corporation claims the full $100,000 Section 41 tax credit, but must reduce its $1,000,000 Section 174A deduction by $100,000 to $900,000. The $900,000 deduction yields a federal tax shield of $900,000 × 21% = $189,000, which combined with the $100,000 tax credit produces a total federal tax benefit of $189,000 + $100,000 = $289,000. However, federal taxable income is $100,000 higher, increasing state income tax liability unless the state provides a specific subtraction modification for Section 280C(c) reductions. Conversely, if the corporation makes the reduced credit election under Section 280C(c)(3), it receives a net Section 41 credit of $100,000 × (1 − 0.21) = $79,000 while retaining the full $1,000,000 Section 174A deduction. The $1,000,000 deduction yields a federal tax shield of $1,000,000 × 21% = $210,000, which combined with the $79,000 net credit produces the exact same federal tax benefit of $210,000 + $79,000 = $289,000, while keeping federal taxable income $100,000 lower for state tax apportionment and flow-through purposes and providing a superior result for pass-through entity owners whose individual marginal tax rates under Section 1 exceed the 21% corporate rate, up to 37%. With 100% immediate expensing restored in 2025, making the Section 280C(c)(3) reduced credit election once again becomes mathematically advantageous for virtually all domestic C corporations and pass-through entities.

body.text: Statutory Clarification on the 2022–2024 TCJA Period and Late Retroactive 280C Elections

During the mandatory capitalization period from 2022 through 2024, the interaction between Section 174 and Section 280C(c) operated under a markedly different statutory formula. Under the literal text of Section 280C(c)(1) as amended by the TCJA, a taxpayer's capitalized Section 174 account was reduced only by the amount (if any) by which the Section 41 research credit exceeded the current-year amortization deduction allowable for such expenditures. Because a taxpayer's annual amortization deduction (even at the 10% Year 1 midpoint rate) almost always exceeded the Section 41 research credit (which typically ranges from 6% to 10% of QREs), claiming the 100% gross Section 41 credit during 2022–2024 generally resulted in zero reduction to either the current amortization deduction or the capitalized Section 174 basis. Even where a reduction applied, reducing a capitalized basis that was amortized over five years was far less costly in Year 1 than reducing a 100% immediate deduction. Consequently, many businesses and tax practitioners properly forewent the Section 280C(c)(3) reduced credit election on their original 2022, 2023, and 2024 tax returns in order to maximize current cash flow from the 100% gross credit.

This created a severe compliance trap for eligible small businesses electing under the OBBBA to apply Section 174A immediate expensing retroactively to 2022–2024. Under historic law, a Section 280C(c)(3) election had to be made on an original timely filed return and could not be made on an amended return. If a small business claimed the 100% gross credit on its original 2022–2024 returns and subsequently amended those returns to claim 100% immediate expensing under Section 174A, the retroactive reinstatement of the pre-TCJA Section 280C(c)(1) deduction-reduction rule would force the business to reduce its newly restored Section 174A deduction by the full gross credit—generating unexpected taxable income or eroding its Net Operating Loss carryforwards. Revenue Procedure 2025-28 resolves this statutory conflict by explicitly authorizing eligible small businesses that amend their 2022–2024 returns under the retroactive Section 174A election to make a late retroactive Section 280C(c)(3) reduced credit election (or to revoke a previously made Section 280C(c)(3) election), preserving 100% of their restored Section 174A deduction.
State Corporate Income Tax Conformity Dynamics

Federal statutory amendments under the OBBBA do not automatically flow through to all state corporate and pass-through income tax regimes; rather, state-level deductibility depends on each jurisdiction's constitutional and statutory method of conforming to the Internal Revenue Code.
Rolling Conformity versus Static Conformity Jurisdictions

States that levy a corporate net income tax generally fall into two primary categories regarding IRC conformity. Rolling conformity jurisdictions—such as Massachusetts, New York, Illinois, and New Jersey—automatically conform to the Internal Revenue Code as currently enacted and amended by Congress. In these rolling conformity states, unless the state legislature enacts a specific decoupling statute, the OBBBA's restoration of immediate domestic expensing under Section 174A and its 2025/2026 transition recovery provisions apply automatically for state corporate income tax purposes without requiring separate state legislation.

By contrast, static (or fixed-date) conformity jurisdictions—such as California, Texas, Florida, Georgia, and Arizona—conform to the Internal Revenue Code as of a specific historical date established by the state legislature (for example, January 1, 2024, or January 1, 2015). Unless static conformity states that previously updated their conformity dates to adopt the TCJA's Section 174 capitalization rules (such as Florida or Georgia) enact new legislation advancing their IRC conformity dates past July 2025 to incorporate the OBBBA, taxpayers operating in those jurisdictions face a complex federal-state decoupling regime. In such un-updated static states, taxpayers deduct 100% of their domestic R&E costs immediately (and recover 2022–2024 unamortized basis) on their federal returns, but must add back those federal Section 174A deductions on their state returns via Schedule M book-to-tax adjustments and continue amortizing domestic R&E costs over five years on separate state depreciation schedules.
State-Specific Decoupling Precedents

Conversely, several major states had already decoupled from (or never adopted) the TCJA's Section 174 capitalization mandate during the 2022–2024 period, creating the exact inverse compliance dynamic for 2025 and 2026. Specifically, Tennessee enacted explicit decoupling legislation in 2022 to permit continued immediate expensing of R&E expenditures for state excise tax purposes, and Wisconsin similarly enacted legislation allowing continued state-level immediate expensing of Section 174 costs. Likewise, because California conforms to the Internal Revenue Code on a static basis as of January 1, 2015, for most corporate and personal income tax provisions, California never adopted the TCJA's 2017 amendments to Section 174 and permitted 100% immediate expensing of both domestic and foreign R&E expenditures throughout the 2022–2024 period.

For ongoing domestic R&E expenditures incurred in 2025 and subsequent taxable years, the enactment of Section 174A under the OBBBA brings federal law back into alignment with California, Tennessee, and Wisconsin law, eliminating the need for state subtraction modifications on current-year domestic spend (though California continues to differ on foreign R&E, where federal law requires 15-year amortization under Section 174 while California permits immediate deduction). However, a critical compliance trap arises for large taxpayers claiming the federal one-year (2025) or two-year (2025–2026) accelerated recovery of 2022–2024 unamortized domestic basis: because those 2022–2024 R&E expenditures were already deducted 100% on the taxpayer's 2022, 2023, and 2024 California, Tennessee, and Wisconsin state tax returns, allowing the federal Section 481(a) transition deduction to flow through into 2025 or 2026 state taxable income would result in an unlawful double deduction of the same expenses. Consequently, corporate tax departments must execute an offsetting state Schedule M addition modification in 2025 (and 2026 if electing the two-year spread) in California, Tennessee, Wisconsin, and any other decoupled state to back out the federal legacy basis recovery.

body.text: Hypothetical Case Studies and Recomputed Quantitative Scenarios

To illustrate the operational, procedural, and quantitative impact of the OBBBA and Revenue Procedure 2025-28 across distinct corporate profiles, the following three hypothetical scenarios apply statutory thresholds, tax rates, and amortization conventions.
Hypothetical Case Study 1: Pre-Revenue Biotechnology Startup (Small Business Retroactivity)

In this first hypothetical scenario, "BioGen Inc." is a venture-backed, pre-revenue biotechnology startup developing a novel monoclonal antibody therapeutic candidate. BioGen generated $0 in commercial revenue and incurred $5,000,000 annually in qualifying domestic R&E expenditures across 2022, 2023, and 2024 ($15,000,000 cumulative domestic R&E spend). Under the pre-OBBBA TCJA regime, BioGen was required to capitalize each annual $5,000,000 vintage over five years using the midpoint convention (10% in Year 1, 20% in Years 2–5, and 10% in Year 6), deducting only $500,000 in 2022, $1,500,000 in 2023 ($1,000,000 from the 2022 vintage plus $500,000 from the 2023 vintage), and $2,500,000 in 2024 ($1,000,000 from 2022, $1,000,000 from 2023, and $500,000 from 2024). Thus, across the three-year window, BioGen was permitted to deduct only $4,500,000 cumulatively, trapping the remaining $10,500,000 in an unamortized deferred tax asset and severely restricting its Net Operating Loss (NOL) carryforwards.

Following the July 2025 enactment of the OBBBA, BioGen easily satisfies the ≤ $31,000,000 gross receipts test under Section 448(c) as an Eligible Small Business. BioGen files Form 1120-X amended returns for 2022 and 2023 alongside a superseding return for 2024 (prior to its extended October 15, 2025 filing deadline), attaching to each filing the required statement titled "Filed Pursuant to Section 3.03 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28". By retroactively expensing the entire $15,000,000 of 2022–2024 domestic R&E costs under Section 174A and the Snow v. Commissioner "in connection with" standard, BioGen increases its cumulative 2022–2024 deductions by $10,500,000 and establishes a full $15,000,000 NOL carryforward asset to shelter future milestone payments or commercial profits (or enhance its tax attribute valuation in a pharmaceutical acquisition). Simultaneously, because BioGen claimed the Section 41(h) qualified small business payroll tax credit against its employer OASDI/Medicare taxes in 2022–2024 without making a Section 280C(c)(3) election on its original returns, BioGen executes a late retroactive Section 280C(c)(3) election under Revenue Procedure 2025-28 so that its research credits do not reduce its newly restored $15,000,000 NOL carryforward dollar-for-dollar under Section 280C(c)(1).
Hypothetical Case Study 2: Mid-Sized Software Enterprise (Accelerated Legacy Basis Recovery)

In this second hypothetical scenario, "AppDev Corp" is a mid-sized SaaS enterprise with $100,000,000 in annual gross receipts that incurred $10,000,000 per year in domestic software development costs under Section 174(c)(3) in 2022, 2023, and 2024 ($30,000,000 total) and incurs $12,000,000 in domestic software development costs in 2025. While a rough approximation that ignores the multi-year layering of overlapping vintages might estimate AppDev Corp's unamortized basis at the end of 2024 at "roughly $24 million" (and a resulting 2025 combined deduction of $36 million), a rigorous step-by-step recomputation under the mandatory five-year midpoint convention of IRC Section 174(a)(2)(B) (10% in Year 1, 20% in Years 2 through 5, and 10% in Year 6) demonstrates that the exact unamortized basis as of December 31, 2024, is $21,000,000. Specifically, for the 2022 spend cohort of $10,000,000, AppDev Corp deducted 10% ($1,000,000) in 2022, 20% ($2,000,000) in 2023, and 20% ($2,000,000) in 2024, resulting in cumulative amortization through December 31, 2024 of $5,000,000 (50%) and leaving an unamortized basis of $10,000,000 − $5,000,000 = $5,000,000. For the 2023 spend cohort of $10,000,000, AppDev Corp deducted 10% ($1,000,000) in 2023 and 20% ($2,000,000) in 2024, resulting in cumulative amortization through December 31, 2024 of $3,000,000 (30%) and leaving an unamortized basis of $10,000,000 − $3,000,000 = $7,000,000. For the 2024 spend cohort of $10,000,000, AppDev Corp deducted 10% ($1,000,000) in 2024, resulting in cumulative amortization through December 31, 2024 of $1,000,000 (10%) and leaving an unamortized basis of $10,000,000 − $1,000,000 = $9,000,000. Summing the unamortized balances across all three cohorts yields the exact total unamortized domestic basis at December 31, 2024:

Because AppDev Corp's $100,000,000 average annual revenue exceeds the $31,000,000 Section 448(c) small business threshold, it is statutorily prohibited from amending its 2022–2024 returns. Instead, AppDev Corp files an automatic accounting method change under Revenue Procedure 2025-28 for the 2025 taxable year (benefiting from the automatic waiver of the five-year prior-change scope limitation) to deduct 100% of its $12,000,000 current 2025 domestic software development spend under Section 174A and elects the one-year accelerated recovery for its $21,000,000 unamortized legacy basis. This generates a combined 2025 federal Section 174A deduction of:

At the 21% corporate tax rate, this $33,000,000 deduction produces $6,930,000 in 2025 federal cash tax savings. Alternatively, if AppDev Corp elects the two-year ratable spread to avoid creating an NOL subject to the 80% taxable income limitation under Section 172(a)(2) or to preserve taxable income for expiring tax credits, it deducts $22,500,000 in 2025 ($12,000,000 current spend plus 50% of legacy basis, or $10,500,000) and recovers the remaining $10,500,000 of legacy basis alongside its 2026 current domestic R&E spend in 2026.
Hypothetical Case Study 3: Multinational Manufacturer (Geographic Supply Chain Optimization)

In this third hypothetical scenario, "GlobalMfg" is a multinational industrial manufacturer with $500,000,000 in annual revenue incurring $50,000,000 annually in domestic U.S. engineering expenses and $10,000,000 annually at an R&D prototype testing facility in Munich, Germany. Under the post-OBBBA regime in 2025, GlobalMfg immediately deducts the $50,000,000 of domestic engineering expenditures under Section 174A, but must capitalize the $10,000,000 German testing costs under Section 174(a)(2)(B) and amortize them over 15 years. Year 1 Foreign Deduction = $10,000,000 ÷ 30 = $333,333

Recognizing that Section 174A explicitly defines "domestic" research to include the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and any possession of the United States, GlobalMfg's corporate tax director collaborates with the chief technology officer to evaluate relocating the testing operations from Germany to an industrial park in Puerto Rico. Shifting the $10,000,000 annual testing expenditure to Puerto Rico reclassifies the outlay from a 15-year amortizable foreign asset under Section 174 to an immediately deductible domestic expenditure under Section 174A, increasing GlobalMfg's Year 1 federal tax deduction on that spend from $333,333 to the full $10,000,000—an immediate first-year deduction increase of $9,666,667 (representing $2,030,000 in incremental Year 1 federal cash tax savings at the 21% corporate rate) while also eliminating the Section 174(d) 15-year abandonment lock.

body.text: Strategic Compliance Framework and Actionable Recommendations

Transitioning from the TCJA capitalization regime to the bifurcated Section 174A/174 framework under the OBBBA requires immediate, coordinated execution across corporate tax accounting, software engineering project tracking, and multi-state tax planning.

First, organizations must implement rigorous cost segmentation across both geography and activity type. Enterprise resource planning (ERP) and general ledger systems must deploy distinct cost centers and sub-accounts to separate domestic labor, contractor, and overhead spend (conducted physically within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions) from foreign employee and third-party contractor spend, including auditing the physical work locations of remote and hybrid engineering personnel. Concurrently, technology and SaaS enterprises must apply the substantive criteria of IRS Notice 2023-63 and Revenue Procedure 2000-50 to segregate statutory software development activities (governed by Section 174 and Section 174A) from routine post-release software maintenance, debugging, and off-the-shelf configuration (immediately deductible under Section 162). Accurate isolation of Section 162 software maintenance removes those costs from the Section 174/174A pool entirely, avoiding 15-year capitalization on offshore maintenance work and reducing the base subject to Section 280C(c) adjustments.

Second, corporate tax departments must quantitatively model the competing transition elections authorized by the OBBBA and Revenue Procedure 2025-28 rather than assuming that a 100% immediate deduction in 2025 is optimal in every scenario. Large taxpayers must compare the multi-year tax effect of deducting 100% of their 2022–2024 unamortized domestic basis in 2025 against spreading that legacy deduction ratably across 2025 and 2026. In scenarios where an oversized 2025 deduction would push the corporation into a Net Operating Loss position (whose utilization in subsequent years is capped at 80% of taxable income under Section 172(a)(2) or restricted by Section 382 ownership-change limitations), where lowering 2025 taxable income triggers Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT) liability under Section 59A or compresses the Section 250 FDII deduction, or where current-year taxable income is needed to absorb expiring foreign tax credits or general business credits, electing the two-year transition spread—or making an affirmative Section 174A(c) 60-month capitalization election or Section 59(e) 10-year election—can yield a superior net present value. Similarly, eligible small businesses must weigh the immediate cash refund or NOL benefit of amending 2022, 2023, and 2024 federal and state tax returns prior to the strict July 2026 statutory deadline against the professional compliance fees and extended audit statute of limitations entailed by amended filings.

Third, taxpayers claiming the Section 41 R&D credit must recalibrate their Section 280C(c) election strategy beginning with the 2025 taxable year. With 100% immediate expensing restored for domestic R&E costs under Section 174A, making the Section 280C(c)(3) reduced credit election (retaining 79% of the credit and 100% of the deduction) is once again the mathematically optimal choice for most domestic businesses. Because the Section 280C(c)(3) election for ongoing tax years must be made on an original timely filed return and is irrevocable once filed, tax departments must ensure the election is properly executed on Form 6765 attached to their 2025 returns, and via a late election under Revenue Procedure 2025-28 on any amended 2022–2024 small business returns.

Finally, multi-state enterprises must conduct a comprehensive state tax conformity and nexus review prior to calculating 2025 and 2026 quarterly estimated tax payments and ASC 740 deferred tax provisions. Identifying fixed-date conformity states where the federal Section 174A immediate deduction or legacy basis recovery remains disallowed—as well as decoupled states like California, Tennessee, and Wisconsin where 2022–2024 domestic R&E costs were already expensed in full—enables corporate tax teams to compute accurate Schedule M addition and subtraction modifications and prevent state underpayment or duplicate-deduction penalties.
